e-21424.problem: Given that $\mathcal{L} \left\{t\sin(\omega t) \right\}=\dfrac{2\omega s}{(s^2+\omega^2)^2},$ find the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{-5t}\cdot t\sin(2t)\right\}.$
e-21424.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),$
then
$\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\}  = F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{t\sin(2t) \right\} = \frac{2(2)s}{(s^{2}+2^2)^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-5t}\cdot t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)} & =\frac{2(2)(s+5)}{((s+5)^{2}+{2}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4(s+5)}{((s+5)^{2}+4)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Given that  $L{t\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{{s}^{2}-{\omega }^{2}}{({s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2})^{2}},$ find the Laplace transform $L{{e}^{4t}\cdot t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)}.$

The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
L{t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)}=\frac{{s}^{2}-{3}^{2}}{({s}^{2}+{3}^{2})^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4t}\cdot t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)} & =\frac{(s-4)^{2}-{3}^{2}}{((s-4)^{2}+{3}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(s-4)^{2}-9}{((s-4)^{2}+9)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
L{t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)}=\frac{{s}^{2}-{3}^{2}}{({s}^{2}+{3}^{2})^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4t}\cdot t\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)} & =\frac{(s-4)^{2}-{3}^{2}}{((s-4)^{2}+{3}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(s-4)^{2}-9}{((s-4)^{2}+9)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Setting ω=5 gives F(s)=10s/(s²+25)². By the first shifting theorem, multiplication by e^{3t} replaces s with s−3 throughout F(s), giving option e.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Given that $L{t\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{2\omega s}{({s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2})^{2}},$ find the Laplace transform $L{{e}^{3t}\cdot t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)}.$
after.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
L{t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)}=\frac{2(5)s}{({s}^{2}+{5}^{2})^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}\cdot t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)} & =\frac{2(5)(s-3)}{((s-3)^{2}+{5}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{10(s-3)}{((s-3)^{2}+25)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Given that $L{t\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{2\omega s}{({s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2})^{2}},$ find the Laplace transform $L{{e}^{3t}\cdot t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)}.$
content.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

Using the given result, we have

$$
L{t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)}=\frac{2(5)s}{({s}^{2}+{5}^{2})^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, applying the first shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}\cdot t\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)} & =\frac{2(5)(s-3)}{((s-3)^{2}+{5}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{10(s-3)}{((s-3)^{2}+25)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$
